name: History of Public Education
description: Public education in Iran developed through local school initiatives, constitutional legislation, and the expansion of a centralized national system. Its history combines wider access to schooling with continuing disputes over curriculum, authority, and educational inequality.

seo.title: History of Public Education in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: How local school initiatives became a national education system, and why access, curriculum, and equality developed unevenly.

content.heading: From educational reform to public schooling
content.content:
Iran's modern public-school system emerged gradually from initiatives with different purposes and constituencies. Dar al-Funun, the polytechnic established in Tehran in 1851 by the reforming minister Amir Kabir, initially trained elite students for technical, military, and medical work. Its importance should not be confused with universal elementary provision: training officials and educating an entire population were different projects. [s1]

Elementary-school pioneers widened that ambition. Hasan Roshdiyeh established a modern primary school in Tabriz in 1888 and subsequently worked in Tehran. The Anjoman-e Maaref, an educational association formed in 1897, helped establish and supervise schools. Early institutions lacked a common curriculum and standardized teaching materials; their founders exercised considerable authority. Schools serving religious minorities and other local constituencies were also part of this varied educational landscape. [s2]

content.heading: An entitlement before universal delivery
content.content:
The Fundamental Law of Education, enacted in 1911 by the Majles, Iran's parliament, required parents or guardians to arrange education for children from age seven and made instruction in public primary schools free. Yet the law itself distinguished village schools from urban schools. Smaller villages could have shorter courses and teachers with fewer educational qualifications. Public responsibility therefore developed within an unequal geography of provision. A legal requirement did not establish that every child could attend an adequately staffed school. [s2]

During the 1920s and 1930s, state centralization brought greater administrative integration and expanding enrollment. Nevertheless, the resulting system remained disproportionately urban and socially selective. Later expansion, especially after the Second World War, extended elementary schooling into rural areas. Ahmad Ashraf's historical survey emphasizes that access and literacy improved while differences between regions, women and men, and rural and urban populations persisted. [s1]

content.heading: Revolution, reconstruction, and competing objectives
content.content:
The 1979 revolution changed education's declared political and cultural purposes. In her study of 1979–95, education scholar Golnar Mehran describes textbook revision and an explicit effort to form citizens committed to Islamic and revolutionary values. Her account also documents expanded educational opportunities, particularly outside cities. Ideological change and broader participation occurred together; one cannot be used as a substitute measure for the other. [s3]

Mehran distinguishes the revolutionary and wartime period from the reconstruction years following the 1988 cease-fire with Iraq. During reconstruction, official priorities placed greater emphasis on skilled workers, educational quality, and reform of secondary schooling. These are documented historical priorities, rather than proof that the intended improvements were achieved everywhere. [s3]

This history is best read through separate questions: who entered school, what they learned, who controlled instruction, and what opportunities followed. Those questions prevent school expansion from becoming a simple success narrative and prevent political changes from obscuring families' growing participation in education. The evidence summarized here establishes the main historical transitions through the mid-1990s; it does not establish conditions in schools at the research cutoff. [s1][s3]

name: Internal Migration through History
description: Internal migration redistributes people within Iran and includes movement between cities, between villages, and across the rural–urban boundary. Census-based evidence documents a growing urban-to-urban share, while changes in measurement complicate comparisons across time.

seo.title: Internal Migration through Iranian History | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iran's changing migration patterns, the rise of movement between cities, and the limits of census comparisons.

content.heading: Movement within the country
content.content:
Internal migration concerns changes of residence within Iran. It must be distinguished from immigration into the country and emigration abroad. It also differs from urbanization: an increase in the population classified as urban does not, by itself, reveal how many people moved. The historical demographic literature identifies changes in the definition of a city and the incorporation of villages into cities as additional reasons urban population totals can increase. [s1]

Measurement matters just as much as geography. Comparing birthplace with residence identifies a different population from asking whether someone moved during a specified interval. Iran's census history illustrates the problem: the 1996 questionnaire omitted birthplace, interrupting the ability to quantify lifetime migrants using that question. Such a break should not be interpreted as evidence that migration itself diminished. [s1]

content.heading: Beyond the village-to-city narrative
content.content:
Migration is often imagined as a single journey from a village to a large city. That pathway matters, but it does not describe the whole system. A historical table reproduced in a KNOMAD report shows an increasing urban-to-urban share across successive reporting intervals. The chart below preserves those intervals rather than presenting the observations as annual measurements. [s2]

The composition of migration and its volume answer different questions. A larger share of moves between urban places does not establish a larger total number of migrants, greater travel distances, or movement exclusively toward Tehran. Nor does this table identify how often an individual moved, whether a move was temporary, or whether a household subsequently returned. [s2]

The report's account of the 2011–2016 period also identifies contrasting provincial experiences: Semnan, Alborz, and Yazd had high positive migration rates, while Lorestan, Chaharmahal-Bakhtiari, and Ilam had high negative rates. This regional variation is more informative than assuming a uniform national experience. [s2]

content.title: Urban-to-urban share of internal migration in Iran
content.x_axis_label: Source reporting interval; intervals have unequal lengths
content.interpretation: The reproduced table reports an urban-to-urban share of 40% in 1976–1986 and 68% in 2011–2016. These are interval shares, not annual migration rates or counts. [s2]

content.heading: Why people move, and what remains uncertain
content.content:
UNFPA's publication introduction describes several motives, including employment, leaving deprivation, retirement, and seeking a different residential environment. Its examples include movement away from cities as well as toward them. This framing helps explain why a single rural-push or urban-pull story is insufficient, although the introduction alone cannot establish the relative importance of each motive. [s3]

Environmental conditions also deserve careful treatment. A CESifo working paper using provincial census evidence from 2011 and 2016 reports a positive relationship between aerosol optical depth, a satellite-based pollution measure, and net outmigration. That statistical finding concerns aggregate provincial patterns; it does not identify the reason for every household's move. [s4]

Read together, these sources support a history of changing destinations and multiple motivations. They also show why contemporary claims require fresh evidence: retrospective census intervals and a later targeted survey cannot supply a continuous national annual migration series. Earlier historical mobility and post-2016 national patterns remain research gaps in this account. [s1][s2]

name: History of Science & Technology
description: Iran's scientific and technological history includes mathematical research, medical writing, hydraulic engineering, and the reproduction of knowledge in manuscripts and print. These developments belonged to multilingual networks extending beyond modern national borders, and their surviving evidence varies considerably.

seo.title: History of Science & Technology in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore scientific learning, medicine, astronomy, qanat engineering, and printing through documented objects, institutions, and debates.

content.heading: Knowledge across languages and borders
content.content:
A useful history of science in Iran follows people, texts, instruments, and working practices. The Library of Congress's Persian-book exhibition shows why language and geography must be distinguished: scholars of Persian origin often wrote scientific works in Arabic, while Persian scientific writing circulated beyond Iran, including at the Mughal court in India. A Persian-language manuscript is therefore evidence of a linguistic network, not automatically an object produced within today's Iranian borders. [s1]

The exhibition also places cosmography beside anatomy, pharmacology, and geography. These materials should be read in their historical categories. A cosmography describing the world's wonders could include mythical creatures; its presence in a scientific collection does not make every description an observation. The surviving book establishes what was written, illustrated, translated, and collected. Assessing the accuracy and practical use of its contents requires further evidence. [s1]

content.heading: Centers of learning: evidence before superlatives
content.content:
Gondeshapur, also spelled Jondeshapur, in southwestern Iran is frequently presented as a great ancient medical university. The institutional scale implied by that description is disputed. Encyclopaedia Iranica's discussion of Greek medicine challenges claims for a great teaching hospital and a uniquely dominant channel carrying Greek medicine to Baghdad. It instead situates the city among several centers of Syriac scholarship where medicine was taught and practiced. [s2]

This distinction matters for the history of medicine and for the branch on ancient learning. The existence of scholarly and medical activity does not establish a modern university structure, a precise founding date, or a claim to be the world's first university. The responsible question is which activities and relationships particular sources document. An overview can acknowledge the city's importance while leaving disputed institutional reconstructions open. [s2]

content.heading: Astronomy as collaborative research
content.content:
Maragha, in northwestern Iran, offers a more closely documented institutional example. Construction of its observatory began in 1259 under the patronage of the Mongol ruler Hulegu. Historian George Saliba places its operation around 1261–62 and describes Nasir al-Din Tusi's collaboration with astronomers and instrument specialists, including Muayyad al-Din al-Urdi from Damascus. [s3]

The work involved more than recording positions in the sky. Researchers examined inherited planetary models and developed mathematical alternatives to particular features of Greek astronomy. Tusi also reworked earlier mathematical texts, comparing translations and revising explanations. This makes the observatory a useful meeting point for astronomy, mathematics, instruments, and patronage. Its achievements arose from a research community, rather than from an isolated genius working outside political and material circumstances. [s3]

content.heading: Engineering below the surface
content.content:
A qanat is a gently sloping underground water channel that draws from an aquifer and carries water by gravity toward settlements and fields. UNESCO's description explains how access shafts support excavation and ventilation, while the tunnel's gradient requires specialized knowledge. Engineering here includes construction, maintenance, and the organization of water distribution. [s4]

The Persian Qanat World Heritage property represents selected systems, rather than every qanat in Iran. Its documentation connects hydraulic structures with reservoirs, mills, gardens, and settlement patterns. This is a useful entry into architectural history because buildings and landscapes depended on supporting infrastructure. UNESCO's account describes communal management traditions; it should not be treated as independent proof that every historical or contemporary distribution arrangement was equitable. [s4]

content.heading: Printing changed how knowledge traveled
content.content:
Nineteenth-century lithography reproduced writing from prepared stone surfaces and helped connect established calligraphic skills with mechanical book production. In Iran, booksellers, copyists, and printers participated in a growing trade centered especially on Tehran and Tabriz. The process did not simply erase manuscript culture: copied books and lithographed books continued alongside one another. [s5]

Dar al-Funun, Tehran's modern polytechnic, established a lithographic press after opening in 1851. Its teaching publications included scientific manuals, linking printing with technical education. This branch therefore connects naturally to the histories of medicine and communication: knowledge depended on reproducible teaching materials as well as discoveries. [s5]

Taken together, manuscripts, observatories, water systems, and printing houses suggest complementary ways to explore this history. Each asks who possessed knowledge, how it was tested or applied, and how it reached others. None alone supplies a continuous national measure of scientific achievement. [s1][s3][s4][s5]
